query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered promising for high-heat wear-resistant use and is suitable for thin-film applications; because bulk preparation is expensive, applying it as a coating on a conventional metal is more practical. Earlier studies reported improved wear or mechanical performance from high-entropy-alloy coatings on Al, Ni, and titanium-alloy substrates, and simulations of FeNiCrCoCu on Cu indicated that sliding speed affects tangential and normal forces. Other work associated composition and grain size with changes in wear damage. However, most prior studies examined a limited operating regime or the properties of the alloys themselves rather than the overall wear resistance of coatings under varied thermal conditions. Subject to retaining FeNiCrCoCu as a coating on a Cu matrix, what single intervention could improve its overall wear resistance during sliding across varied thermal and contact regimes? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its causal mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to an unchanged coating in matched tests, the boundaries within which it should hold, supporting evidence from the introduction, and an experiment with a clear rejection criterion for both the predicted outcome and the proposed mechanism.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a controlled volume fraction of stable, coherent L12-type precipitates (e.g., via Al or Ti addition) into the FeNiCrCoCu coating will significantly enhance its wear resistance across varied thermal and contact regimes by providing precipitation strengthening that mitigates thermal softening and suppresses grain boundary sliding.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating deposited on a Cu matrix substrate, initially in a single-phase solid solution state (FCC) with no intentional precipitates, exhibiting standard wear resistance but potential thermal softening at elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor alloying addition of Aluminum (Al) or Titanium (Ti) (e.g., 5-10 at.%) to the FeNiCrCoCu composition prior to coating deposition to induce the formation of coherent L12 precipitates (γ') within the FCC matrix.
generation.conditions: Sliding contact tests conducted across a varied thermal regime (e.g., room temperature to 400°C) and varied contact regimes (varying sliding speeds and normal loads), simulating high-heat wear-resistant applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent L12 (Ni3Al or Ni3Ti) precipitates dispersed within the FCC matrix, acting as obstacles to dislocation motion and stabilizing the microstructure against thermal coarsening.
generation.mechanism: The precipitates provide precipitation strengthening (Orowan bypassing or shearing mechanisms) which increases yield strength and hardness at elevated temperatures where the single-phase matrix would otherwise soften. This maintains a higher hardness gradient and reduces the rate of abrasive and adhesive wear mechanisms (ploughing and material transfer) that are accelerated by thermal softening and grain boundary sliding.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Al/Ti-modified FeNiCrCoCu coating will exhibit a statistically significant reduction in wear rate (volume loss per unit distance) and a higher retention of surface hardness compared to the unmodified FeNiCrCoCu coating when tested under identical varied thermal and contact conditions, particularly at temperatures >200°C.
generation.baseline: Unmodified FeNiCrCoCu coating on Cu substrate tested under the same varied thermal and contact regimes.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis holds for moderate additions of Al/Ti that maintain a single-phase FCC matrix with coherent precipitates; it may fail if the addition is too high, leading to the formation of brittle complex phases (e.g., B2, Laves, or sigma phases) or loss of ductility, or if the temperature exceeds the solvus temperature of the precipitates causing coarsening.
generation.uncertainty: The specific optimal concentration of Al/Ti required to maximize precipitate density without inducing brittleness in the thin-film coating architecture is not precisely defined in the provided evidence. Additionally, the interaction between the Cu substrate and the modified coating during high-temperature sliding (diffusion) is not fully characterized in the available literature.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings on Cu substrates: Set A (baseline, no Al/Ti) and Set B (modified with 7 at.% Al). Subject both sets to a standardized sliding wear test (pin-on-disk) at a constant load but varying temperatures (25°C, 200°C, 400°C) and sliding speeds. Analyze the microstructure of the worn surfaces and subsurface layers using TEM to confirm precipitate presence and size.
measurements: Wear rate (mm³/N·m) calculated from mass loss and volume displacement
Precipitate volume fraction and size distribution (TEM/SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if Set B (modified) shows no statistically significant improvement in wear rate over Set A at temperatures >200°C, or if TEM analysis reveals that the precipitates have coarsened or dissolved at the test temperatures, or if the modified coating exhibits catastrophic brittle failure (cracking) at lower loads compared to the baseline.

Recent studies have shown attractive mechanical properties of HEAs at cryogenic temperature [4] and room temperature [5] with excellent combinations of high strength and toughness, indicating their potential as the structural materials. High-entropy alloys (HEAs), since their discovery by Yeh et al. in 2004, [1] have opened up researchers to a new alloy system that contains five or more equimolar principal elements. In equimolar HEAs, each element has an equal probability of occupying the lattice sites in a crystal structure such as face-centered cubic (FCC), [2] body-centered cubic (BCC), [3] or hexagonal structure [4] crystal structures. Lattice distortion, sluggish diffusion, high entropy, and cocktail effects have been identified as the core effects contributing to the superior properties, hardness, strength, ductility, erosion, tribocorrosion, corrosion, and oxidation/wear resistance [5] − [7] of HEAs in a wide range of temperatures over conventional alloys. From the viewpoint of applications in extrusion dies and cutting inserts, the cost of metal powders used to develop bulk HEAs can hinder their commercialization as an alternative to the alloys in use. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) present a new approach of alloying concepts. Whereas conventional alloys usually comprise one major alloying element and minor additions of other alloying elements to improve properties, HEAs consist of at least five elements with close to equimolar composition. For several compositions, the desired formation of solely solid solutions with a face-centred cubic (fcc) or a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure could be achieved [ [1] , [2] , [3] ].

Several groups of HEAs have been intensively investigated. The term compositionally complex alloys (CCAs) was introduced for HEAs with a multiphase microstructure [ [4] ]. Several investigations prove the formation of primarily cubic phases in the alloy AlCoCrCuFeNi and its derivatives [ [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Aluminium strongly influences the microstructure, phase formation and resulting properties. Furthermore, aluminium acts as a stabiliser of bcc solid solutions and can suppress the formation of complex phases [ [8] , [9] , [10] ].
